title: American Cyclist Brandon McNulty Stuns Field to Win World Road Race Title in Montreal
summary: Brandon McNulty wasn't supposed to win. The 28-year-old American wasn't among the pre-race favourites at the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal on Sunday — not like former world champion Remco Evenepoel or young stars Isaac del Toro and Paul Seixas. But with 33 kilometres left in the 273.4-kilometre race, he made his move — and nobody could catch him. McNulty crossed the line in 6 hours, 17 minutes and 4 seconds, becoming the first American to win the elite road race world title since Lance Armstrong in 1993. "Until the last 300 metres, I really didn't even believe it," McNulty said. "I was just dying, but I just kept pushing." He added: "I'm at a loss for words." The race was chaotic from the start. Two-time defending champion Tadej Pogacar of Slovenia was absent, recovering from a crash, which left the field wide open. The course included 12 laps of a 13.4-kilometre circuit packed with enthusiastic fans. McNulty struggled on the final significant climb and saw his lead shrink to just 10 seconds with 10 kilometres to go. But none of the chasers could take advantage — Matthew van der Poel of the Netherlands led an attack with 6.8 kilometres left, but it fizzled out. Michael Matthews of Australia took silver in 6:17:17, and van der Poel earned bronze. "We've said for weeks that we have a super strong team and that it's possible. We rode crazy well. We marked everything, had guys ahead," McNulty said. "I knew something could happen but it would take a miracle. I guess today, a miracle happened." Michael Leonard of Oakville, Ont., was the top Canadian in 32nd place in 6:23:43. Michael Woods of Toronto finished 35th in 6:23:52 in his final race. Armstrong congratulated McNulty on his victory.
why_it_matters: This story shows that favourites are only predictions, not results: a rider nobody expected to win took the title because his whole team stuck to a plan and kept believing when the gap was shrinking. The same idea applies to group projects and school teams — the strongest-looking side does not always finish first.

background_read: The UCI Road World Championships (the yearly world-title races run by the Union Cycliste Internationale, cycling's global governing body) end with a one-day road race in which the winner earns the right to wear the rainbow jersey for a whole year.

Unlike the Tour de France (the three-week stage race that is cycling's most famous event), the world road race is decided in a single afternoon, so riders cannot relax and wait for another day to make up time.

Tadej Pogacar (the Slovenian star who has won the Tour de France several times) was missing from this race while recovering from a crash, which threw the race open to riders who normally ride in his shadow.

Lance Armstrong (the American who won seven Tour de France titles before they were stripped from him in a doping scandal) had been the last American to take this title, back in 1993, so McNulty's win ended a very long wait.

Montreal (the largest city in the Canadian province of Quebec) hosted this edition, and the course sent riders around the same 13.4-kilometre loop of city streets twelve times, with big crowds lining the route.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — American cycling gets a boost
perspectives.description: McNulty ends a wait that stretches back to 1993, giving American riders a new role model and drawing sponsors and young talent toward the sport. A homegrown world champion can do more for a national cycling programme than years of steady results.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the title came without the biggest name
perspectives.description: Two-time defending champion Tadej Pogacar was absent after a crash, so some fans will argue the rainbow jersey was decided in a weakened field. On top of that, the last American to hold this title was Lance Armstrong, whose doping scandal makes any comparison awkward.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — one-day racing rewards long-range gambles
perspectives.description: In a single-day championship there is no tomorrow, so bold attacks from far out succeed far more often than they do in three-week stage races where teams can chase calmly. World championships have a long history of crowning surprise winners who timed one perfect move.

The win changes how other teams will race against McNulty, who now carries the rainbow jersey and the pressure that comes with it. The bigger question is whether this can translate into wider investment in American junior and development cycling, or stays a one-off celebration.
